story: Amira and Daniel married in Kingston in 2014 and separated in March 2025 with no prospect of getting back together. During the marriage Amira's aunt left her $90,000 in her will. Amira used $60,000 of it to pay down the mortgage on the house the couple lived in, which is in both names, and kept the other $30,000 in a separate savings account that still holds it. In 2021 Amira also received a $40,000 settlement for damages for her personal injuries after a car accident. Daniel owns a 2019 pickup truck he bought during the marriage, and he keeps the family dog.
question: In working out Amira's net family property for equalization, which of these amounts are left out, and does it matter that part of the inheritance went into the house?
modelAnswer: Under the Family Law Act, Part I, some property a spouse owns on the valuation date does not form part of net family property (s. 4 (2)). Property acquired by gift or inheritance from a third person after the date of the marriage is excluded, but only if it is not a matrimonial home (s. 4 (2), para. 1). Property into which excluded property can be traced is also excluded, again other than a matrimonial home (para. 5). So the $30,000 still held in the separate account can be excluded as traced inheritance, but the $60,000 put into the matrimonial home does not keep its excluded status: the home is the exception the Act names. Damages for personal injuries, or the part of a settlement that represents those damages, are excluded (para. 3), so the accident settlement, to the extent it represents those damages, is left out. The person claiming an exclusion has to prove it (s. 4 (3)), so Amira needs records tracing the inheritance and showing what the settlement was for. Daniel's truck and the dog are not exclusions; they are simply part of whatever property each spouse owns on the valuation date.
keyPoints: inheritance after marriage is excluded
but not if it is a matrimonial home
traced property is excluded except a matrimonial home
personal injury damages are excluded
onus on the person claiming the exclusion

sources.quote: Property, other than a matrimonial home, that was acquired by gift or inheritance from a third person after the date of the marriage.
Damages or a right to damages for personal injuries, nervous shock, mental distress or loss of guidance, care and companionship, or the part of a settlement that represents those damages.
Property, other than a matrimonial home, into which property referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 can be traced.
The onus of proving a deduction under the definition of “net family property” or an exclusion under subsection (2) is on the person claiming it.

story: Grace and Tomas separated in June 2019 in Sudbury, with no reasonable prospect of reconciling. They never divorced. Grace moved to Thunder Bay, started a new job and put off dealing with the property because talks with Tomas kept stalling. In 2026 she learns that Tomas's pension and RRSPs grew a great deal during the marriage and wants to claim an equalization payment.
question: What time limit applies to Grace's equalization claim, what starts it running, and does the Act give any way to bring the claim late?
modelAnswer: An application for equalization under s. 5 (1) of the Family Law Act cannot be brought after the earliest of: two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity; six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation; or six months after the first spouse's death (s. 7 (3)). Grace and Tomas are not divorced and both are alive, so the period that applies is six years from the June 2019 separation. If that period has run out, the Act lets the court, on motion, extend a time it prescribes if it is satisfied that there are apparent grounds for relief, that relief is unavailable because of delay incurred in good faith, and that no person will suffer substantial prejudice because of the delay (s. 2 (8)). Grace would have to show all three. If a divorce were later granted, the two-year period after the divorce would also have to be watched, since the earliest date governs.
keyPoints: earliest of the listed dates
six years after separation with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation
two years after divorce
six months after a spouse's death
court may extend: apparent grounds, good-faith delay, no substantial prejudice

two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity;
six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation; (c) six months after the first spouse’s death.

The court may, on motion, extend a time prescribed by this Act if it is satisfied that, (a) there are apparent grounds for relief; (b) relief is unavailable because of delay that has been incurred in good faith; and (c) no person will suffer substantial prejudice by reason of the delay.

question: Under Ontario's Family Law Act, what is the 'valuation date' used to calculate net family property, and at what time of day on that date are values fixed?
modelAnswer: The valuation date is the earliest of five dates (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1)): (1) the date the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation; (2) the date a divorce is granted; (3) the date the marriage is declared a nullity; (4) the date one spouse starts an application based on s. 5 (3) (improvident depletion) that is later granted; and (5) the date before the date on which one spouse dies leaving the other surviving. When a value must be calculated as of a given date, it is calculated as of close of business on that date (s. 4 (4)).
keyPoints: the earliest of the listed dates
separation with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation
divorce, nullity, improvident depletion application, day before death
close of business

story: Raj bought a townhouse in Mississauga in his own name two years before he married Leena. They lived there together as a family for eight years. Last month they separated and Leena is staying in the townhouse with their son while Raj sleeps at his brother's. Raj has had an offer from a buyer and has also asked a locksmith about changing the locks.
question: Since the townhouse is only in Raj's name, he can sell it or lock Leena out whenever he likes, right? What does he need to know?
modelAnswer: No. Ownership is not the test. Under the Family Law Act, property in which a person has an interest and that was ordinarily occupied by the spouses as their family residence at the time of separation is their matrimonial home (s. 18 (1)), whoever holds title. Both spouses have an equal right to possession of a matrimonial home (s. 19 (1)); where only one spouse has an interest, the other's right is personal against that spouse and ends when they cease to be spouses unless a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise (s. 19 (2)). Raj cannot sell or mortgage his interest in the matrimonial home unless Leena joins in or consents, she has released her rights by a separation agreement, a court order authorizes it, or a registered designation of another property applies (s. 21 (1)). A sale made in breach of that can be set aside, except against someone who acquired the interest for value, in good faith and without notice that it was a matrimonial home (s. 21 (2)). Either spouse can apply for an order about possession, including exclusive possession (s. 24 (1)). Note also that the home's value is not deducted as pre-marriage property: the deduction for property owned on the date of marriage is for property 'other than a matrimonial home' (s. 4 (1)).

both spouses have an equal right to possession
cannot dispose of or encumber without the other's consent, release or court order

story: Since separating in August, Joanne and Pierre have kept living under the same roof in their Ottawa house with their two children, ages 6 and 9. Pierre has twice thrown dishes during arguments and Joanne and the children are frightened. Joanne earns less than Pierre and says rents near the children's school are beyond her means. Pierre says he paid the whole down payment and the house is really his. Joanne wants an order that she and the children can stay in the house and Pierre must leave while the case goes on.
question: What order can Joanne ask for, can she get it before the case is finished, and what must the court consider in deciding it? What document must accompany her claim?
modelAnswer: Regardless of who owns the matrimonial home, the court may on application direct that one spouse be given exclusive possession of the matrimonial home or part of it for the period the court directs (Family Law Act, s. 24 (1) (b)), so Pierre's down payment does not answer the question. The court may make a temporary or interim order of this kind on motion (s. 24 (2)). In deciding whether to order exclusive possession, the court must consider the best interests of the children affected; existing property and support orders; the financial position of both spouses; any written agreement; the availability of other suitable and affordable accommodation; and any violence committed by a spouse against the other spouse or the children (s. 24 (3)). For the children's best interests the court considers the possible disruptive effects of a move and the children's views and preferences if they can reasonably be ascertained (s. 24 (4)). Under the Family Law Rules, a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home must be served and filed with a financial statement (r. 13 (1)), in Form 13.1 (r. 13 (1.2)). Contravening an exclusive possession order is an offence (s. 24 (5)).

story: Nadia and Owen never married. They lived together in Hamilton for two years and four months and have a 14-month-old daughter, Ivy. Nadia left her job at a bank to care for Ivy. When they split up, Owen told her: 'We weren't married and it wasn't even three years, so you have no right to support from me.' Nadia's friend Carla, who lived with her own partner for four years with no children, wonders whether she would be in the same position.
question: Is Nadia a 'spouse' who can claim spousal support under Ontario's Family Law Act? Would Carla be?
modelAnswer: For support, Part III of the Family Law Act uses a wider definition of spouse than the property part. A spouse includes married persons and, in addition, two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited either continuously for a period of not less than three years, or in a relationship of some permanence if they are the parents of a child as set out in s. 4 of the Children's Law Reform Act (s. 29). Owen is mistaken that three years is the only route: Nadia and Owen are Ivy's parents, so the question is whether theirs was a relationship of some permanence. Carla, with no child, would come within the definition through continuous cohabitation of not less than three years. Being a spouse is the threshold; every spouse has an obligation to provide support for himself or herself and for the other spouse, in accordance with need, to the extent he or she is capable (s. 30), and the amount and duration are decided on the factors in s. 33 (9).
keyPoints: s. 29 extended definition for support
three years of continuous cohabitation
relationship of some permanence if parents of a child

story: Helen and Marcus were married for 22 years and live in London, Ontario. Helen stayed home to raise their three children and run the household while Marcus built a career as an engineer; she has not worked outside the home since 2004. Their youngest is now 19, has a disability and still lives with Helen. Marcus left the marriage for a new partner, and Helen is hurt and angry and wants the court to 'punish' him through support. Marcus says Helen should just get a job, since she is only 51.
question: On what bases can Helen claim spousal support, what does the court look at in setting the amount and duration under the Family Law Act, and does Marcus leaving for someone else count?
modelAnswer: The Supreme Court in Bracklow v. Bracklow held that the law recognizes three conceptual grounds for entitlement to spousal support: compensatory, contractual and non-compensatory (para. 15). Under the Family Law Act, an order for spousal support should recognize the spouse's contribution to the relationship and its economic consequences for the spouse, share the economic burden of child support equitably, make fair provision to assist the spouse to become able to contribute to her own support, and relieve financial hardship (s. 33 (8)). In setting amount and duration, the court considers all the circumstances, including the parties' assets and means now and in the future, the dependant's capacity to contribute to her own support, the respondent's capacity to pay, age and health, needs measured against the accustomed standard of living, the measures available for her to become self-supporting and their time and cost, and, for a spouse, the length of cohabitation, the effect on earning capacity of responsibilities assumed during cohabitation, whether she has undertaken the care of a child 18 or over who is unable because of disability to withdraw from parental charge, housekeeping and child care performed for the family, and the effect of caring for a child on her earnings and career (s. 33 (9)). Marcus's point about Helen working goes to her capacity and the measures available to become self-supporting; it is a factor, not the whole test. As for his leaving: the obligation exists without regard to the conduct of either spouse, and the court may have regard only to a course of conduct so unconscionable as to constitute an obvious and gross repudiation of the relationship (s. 33 (10)). Support is not a means of punishment.

question: Under the Ontario Child Support Guidelines, what is the presumptive amount of child support for children under the age of majority, and what does it depend on?
modelAnswer: A court making a child support order under the Family Law Act must do so in accordance with the child support guidelines (s. 33 (11)). Unless the guidelines provide otherwise, the amount for children under the age of majority is (a) the amount set out in the applicable table, according to the number of children under the age of majority to whom the order relates and the income of the parent against whom the order is sought, and (b) the amount, if any, determined under s. 7 for special or extraordinary expenses (Ontario Child Support Guidelines, s. 3 (1)). Where the paying parent's income is over $150,000, the court may depart from the table for the income above $150,000 if it considers the table amount inappropriate (s. 4). Other exceptions include shared parenting time of at least 40 per cent (s. 9) and undue hardship (s. 10).

story: Simone has the majority of parenting time with her two children in Barrie. She earns $48,000 a year and their father, Kwame, earns $96,000 and pays table child support. This year their 13-year-old needs braces costing $6,200, of which Simone's workplace insurance covers $1,500. Their 10-year-old plays competitive rep hockey costing $5,800 a season, much more than the house league she played in while the parents lived together. Simone works full time and pays $9,000 a year for after-school care. Kwame says table support 'covers everything'.
question: Can Simone ask for help with these costs on top of table support, and how would any amount be shared?
modelAnswer: Yes, she can ask. Section 7 of the Ontario Child Support Guidelines lets the court, on the request of either parent, provide an amount to cover all or part of listed expenses, taking into account the necessity of the expense in relation to the child's best interests and its reasonableness in relation to the parents' and child's means and the family's spending pattern during cohabitation (s. 7 (1)). The listed expenses include child care costs incurred because of the employment of the parent with the majority of parenting time (s. 7 (1) (a)) — the after-school care; health-related expenses that exceed insurance reimbursement by at least $100 annually, including orthodontic treatment (s. 7 (1) (c)) — the braces, net of the $1,500 coverage; and extraordinary expenses for extracurricular activities (s. 7 (1) (f)) — the rep hockey, which must meet the definition of 'extraordinary expenses' in s. 7 (1.1), looking at the cost relative to the requesting parent's income and table support, the child's special needs and talents, and the overall cost. The guiding principle is that the expense is shared in proportion to the parents' respective incomes, after deducting any contribution from the child (s. 7 (2)). With incomes of $48,000 and $96,000, that is one third to Simone and two thirds to Kwame. The court must also take into account any subsidies, benefits or tax deductions or credits relating to the expense (s. 7 (3)).

story: Dmitri pays table child support for his two children with his former partner in Windsor. He has since remarried and has a baby with his new wife, and he is still paying off a large line of credit the couple ran up to cover family expenses before they separated. His former partner lives in a modest apartment; Dmitri and his new wife own a house. He is preparing a claim to pay less than the table amount because of undue hardship.
question: I'm under so much financial pressure. Is my undue hardship claim strong enough that the court will lower my support?
modelAnswer: The site does not judge whether a claim will work or how a court will decide it; it can set out what the Guidelines require so you can prepare. Under s. 10 (1) of the Ontario Child Support Guidelines, the court may award an amount different from the table amount if it finds that the parent making the request, or a child, would otherwise suffer undue hardship. Circumstances that may cause undue hardship include an unusually high level of debts reasonably incurred to support the family during cohabitation or to earn a living, and a legal duty to support a child other than the child who is the subject of the application who is under the age of majority (s. 10 (2) (a), (e)) — both match facts you describe. There is a second step: even if undue hardship is found, the application must be denied if the household of the parent claiming it would, after child support is set, have a higher standard of living than the other parent's household (s. 10 (3)). The court may use the household standard of living comparison test in Schedule II (s. 10 (4)). So what has to be shown is the hardship circumstance itself, that it amounts to undue hardship, and a comparison of the two households' standards of living; that means gathering evidence of the debt and its purpose, your new household's income (including your spouse's), and expenses. Next step: prepare your financial statement and the standard of living comparison.

story: Lucia and Ben separated in 2018, and Ben agreed to pay $500 a month for their son. In February 2021 Lucia texted Ben: 'You got promoted — we need to talk about raising support.' Ben did not answer and nothing changed. Lucia served Ben with an application to increase support in September 2026. It turns out Ben's income had already doubled in 2019 and he never told Lucia, despite their agreement requiring yearly income disclosure.
question: How far back can a retroactive increase in child support reach, what starts the period, and does Ben's failure to disclose change the starting point?
modelAnswer: The Family Law Act lets a support order require support for a period before the date of the order (s. 34 (1) (f)). The Supreme Court in D.B.S. v. S.R.G. adopted the date of effective notice as the general starting point: 'effective notice' means any indication by the recipient parent that support should be paid or that the current amount needs to be renegotiated; it does not require legal action, only that the topic be broached (para. 121). Lucia's February 2021 text is that kind of indication. The Court added that it will usually be inappropriate to make an award retroactive to a date more than three years before formal notice was given to the payor (para. 123); here formal notice was September 2026. But where the payor engages in blameworthy conduct, including not disclosing a material increase in income, the presumptive date moves back to when circumstances changed materially (para. 124). In Colucci v. Colucci the Court confirmed that the date of effective notice is not relevant when a payor has engaged in blameworthy conduct, including failure to disclose material information (para. 42). So Ben's non-disclosure of his 2019 increase bears directly on the start date; the court still decides on all the circumstances, including the reasons for any delay, the payor's conduct, the child's circumstances and hardship.
keyPoints: date of effective notice as the general rule
effective notice only requires broaching the topic
usually no more than three years before formal notice
blameworthy conduct moves the date to the material change
non-disclosure of an income increase is blameworthy conduct

Not disclosing a material change in circumstances — including an increase in income that one would expect to alter the amount of child support payable — is itself blameworthy conduct. The presence of such blameworthy conduct will move the presumptive date of retroactivity back to the time when circumstances changed materially.

story: Aisha and Kevin, who were never married, are separating in Brampton. Their children are 4 and 11. Kevin has been the one who drives the children to school and coaches the 11-year-old's soccer team; Aisha handled medical appointments and homework. Over the last year Kevin has checked Aisha's phone, controlled all the money and told her she could not see her friends; the 11-year-old has overheard many of these arguments. Kevin points out that Aisha had an affair years ago and says that should count against her. The 11-year-old has told a teacher she wants to live with both parents. Both want decision-making responsibility.
question: What does the court consider in deciding decision-making responsibility and parenting time, how does Kevin's controlling behaviour fit in, and is Aisha's past affair relevant?
modelAnswer: Because the parents were not married, the Children's Law Reform Act applies. In making a parenting order the court takes into account only the best interests of the child, and it must give primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being (s. 24 (1), (2)). The factors include the children's needs given their age and stage of development, their relationships with each parent and others, each parent's willingness to support the children's relationship with the other parent, the history of care, the child's views and preferences given due weight to age and maturity, plans for care, each person's ability to care for the children and to communicate and co-operate, and any family violence and its impact (s. 24 (3)). 'Family violence' includes conduct that constitutes a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour and, for a child, direct or indirect exposure to such conduct (s. 18 (1)). In weighing family violence the court takes into account its nature, seriousness and frequency, whether there is a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour, whether the child is directly or indirectly exposed, and any steps taken by the person to prevent further violence (s. 24 (4)). Past conduct is not considered unless it is relevant to the exercise of the person's decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact (s. 24 (5)), so an affair years ago is not a factor unless it bears on parenting. The court allocates parenting time on the principle that a child should have as much time with each parent as is consistent with the child's best interests (s. 24 (6)).

story: Priya and Mateo, who never married, share parenting time for their 7-year-old son under a court order made in Toronto under the Children's Law Reform Act. Priya has been offered a nursing job in Kenora and wants to move there with their son, starting at the beginning of the next school term. Mateo has heard nothing about it yet.
question: What notice must Priya give before relocating, how far ahead, what must it say, and how long does Mateo have to object? Is there any exception?
modelAnswer: A person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time who intends a relocation must, at least 60 days before the expected date of the proposed relocation, notify any other person who has decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact under a contact order with respect to the child (Children's Law Reform Act, s. 39.3 (1)). The notice must be in the prescribed form or, if none is prescribed, in writing, and must set out the expected date of the relocation, the address of the new residence and contact information, a proposal as to how decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact could be exercised, and any other prescribed information (s. 39.3 (2)). Mateo may object no later than 30 days after receiving the notice, either by notifying Priya of the objection or by making an application under s. 21 (s. 39.3 (5)); a written objection must state that he objects, his reasons, and his views on her proposal (s. 39.3 (6)). Priya may move as of the date in the notice only if a court authorizes it, or if no objection is made in accordance with s. 39.3 (5) and no order prohibits the relocation (s. 39.4 (2)). The exception: on application, which may be made without notice, the court may provide that the notice requirements do not apply or apply with changes, including if there is a risk of family violence (s. 39.3 (3), (4)).

story: Under their divorce order, Elena and Graham's twin daughters, age 10, spend alternate weeks with each parent in Guelph, and both parents have followed that schedule closely for three years. Elena has remarried and wants to move with the girls to Halifax, where her new husband has a job. She gave proper notice and Graham objected in time. Graham's lawyer plans to ask Elena in court whether she would stay in Guelph if the move were refused.
question: Under the Divorce Act, who has to prove what on Elena's relocation request, what extra factors does the court weigh, and can it consider whether Elena would move without the girls?
modelAnswer: Where the parties substantially comply with an order providing that a child spend substantially equal time in the care of each party, the party who intends to relocate the child has the burden of proving that the relocation would be in the best interests of the child (Divorce Act, s. 16.93 (1)). The alternating-week schedule, followed for three years, fits that description, so the burden is on Elena. Besides the s. 16 best-interests factors, the court considers the reasons for the relocation, its impact on the child, the time each parent spends with the child and their involvement, compliance with notice requirements, any order specifying where the child is to live, the reasonableness of the proposal to vary parenting arrangements including travel expenses, and each person's compliance with their obligations (s. 16.92 (1)). The court shall not consider, if the relocation were prohibited, whether the person would relocate without the child or not relocate (s. 16.92 (2)), so the question Graham's lawyer plans to put is about a factor the Act excludes. The Supreme Court in Barendregt v. Grebliunas noted that the Divorce Act now instructs courts to consider the moving parent's reasons for relocation (para. 127).

story: Yusuf and Mariam, married ten years, agreed to separate in November 2025 but kept living in separate bedrooms of their Markham condo until Mariam moved out in February 2026. In April 2026 they tried living together again for six weeks to see if they could reconcile, but it did not work. Neither has done anything wrong; the marriage has simply broken down. Yusuf has read online that you need a three-year separation, or proof of fault, to divorce in Canada.
question: Since nobody is at fault, does Yusuf have to wait three years before he can get a divorce? And did the six weeks back together restart the clock?
modelAnswer: No. The only ground for divorce is breakdown of the marriage (Divorce Act, s. 8 (1)), and breakdown is established if the spouses have lived separate and apart for at least one year immediately preceding the determination of the divorce proceeding and were living separate and apart when it was started (s. 8 (2) (a)). Fault is a different route — adultery or cruelty (s. 8 (2) (b)) — and is not needed. There is no three-year period. Spouses are deemed to have lived separate and apart for any period during which they lived apart and either had the intention to do so (s. 8 (3) (a)). A period of separation is not interrupted or ended by resuming cohabitation for a period, or periods totalling, not more than 90 days with reconciliation as its primary purpose (s. 8 (3) (b) (ii)), so the six-week attempt did not restart the clock. Yusuf can start the proceeding while separated; the one year must be complete by the time the court decides it.

one year separate and apart, not three

story: Claire and Antoine separated in Ottawa in 2023 and have two children, 8 and 12. Antoine has applied for a simple divorce and is planning to remarry in a church ceremony next spring. Claire agrees the marriage is over but says Antoine has been paying only $200 a month for the children since 2023, well below what she understands the table amount would be at his income. Antoine says child support is 'a separate issue' that has nothing to do with the divorce. They also ask when a divorce actually takes effect, because Antoine wants to book his wedding date.
question: Can the divorce be granted while child support is unresolved, and once a divorce judgment is made, when does it take effect?
modelAnswer: Child support is not separate from the divorce in the way Antoine thinks. In a divorce proceeding the court has a duty to satisfy itself that reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage, having regard to the applicable guidelines, and if they have not, to stay the granting of the divorce until they are (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (b)). Arrangements are measured against the guidelines; a court may approve an agreed amount different from the guidelines only if satisfied that reasonable arrangements have been made, and it does not treat them as unreasonable solely because the amount differs from the guideline amount (s. 15.1 (7), (8)). So the court will look at whether $200 a month is a reasonable arrangement in light of the guidelines. The court must also be satisfied there has been no collusion (s. 11 (1) (a)). As for timing, a divorce generally takes effect on the thirty-first day after the day the judgment is rendered (s. 12 (1)); it can take effect earlier only if the court finds special circumstances and the spouses agree and undertake not to appeal (s. 12 (2)). Antoine should not plan to remarry before the divorce has taken effect.

story: Rosa started a family case in the Superior Court of Justice in Oshawa three weeks ago, asking for parenting orders and child support. Her former husband Felix filed an answer. No conference has been held yet. Felix's employer has now transferred him and he has announced he will take the children to Alberta in ten days, though they have lived with Rosa since birth. Separately, Rosa would like an order requiring Felix to produce his tax returns.
question: Can Rosa bring a motion now, before a case conference? What is the general rule and what exceptions apply?
modelAnswer: The general rule under the Family Law Rules is that no notice of motion or supporting evidence may be served and no motion may be heard before a conference dealing with the substantive issues in the case has been completed (r. 14 (4)). That rule does not apply if the court is of the opinion that there is a situation of urgency or hardship, or that a case conference is not required for some other reason in the interest of justice (r. 14 (4.2)). A threatened removal of the children to another province in ten days is the kind of situation for which Rosa would ask the court to find urgency. Rule 14 (6) also lists motions that are not caught, such as motions made without notice, on consent, unopposed or limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters. The disclosure request is not urgent in the same way; ensuring disclosure of relevant evidence, including financial information needed to resolve a support issue, is one of the purposes of a case conference (r. 17 (4) (d)), so it would ordinarily be raised there.

story: On October 1, 2026, Harjit was personally served at his home in Brantford with his wife's family law application. It claims an equalization of net family property, spousal support and child support. Harjit disagrees with almost everything in it but is thinking of not responding at all, because he thinks that if he does not file an answer he will not have to disclose his finances either.
question: How long does Harjit have to answer, and does not answering excuse him from filing a financial statement?
modelAnswer: A person against whom an application is made must serve an answer on every other party and file it within 30 days after being served with the application (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (1)); the period is 60 days only where the application is served outside Canada or the United States (r. 10 (2)), which is not Harjit's situation. Not answering does not avoid financial disclosure. Where an application contains a claim for support or a property claim, the party against whom the claim is made must serve and file a financial statement within the time for serving and filing an answer, whether the party is serving an answer or not (r. 13 (1) (b)). Because the application includes a property claim, the financial statement must be in Form 13.1 (r. 13 (1.2)). The Family Law Act also requires each party in an equalization application to serve and file a sworn statement of property, debts and exclusions (s. 8). The 30 days run from the day he was served; any calendar date should be checked against the Rules' provisions on counting time.

story: Before their wedding in Peterborough, Sofia and Liam typed up a two-page 'prenup' at the kitchen table. Both signed it, but no one else was present. It says: (1) the house Liam owns will be his alone and Sofia gives up any right to live in it if they separate; (2) any children will live with Liam if they separate; (3) neither will ever pay child support to the other. Liam did not mention a $150,000 investment account he held at the time. They have now separated with one child, age 3.
question: Which parts of this agreement can be enforced under the Family Law Act, and on what grounds might it be set aside?
modelAnswer: Several problems arise. First, formalities: a domestic contract is unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed (Family Law Act, s. 55 (1)); a contract signed with no one else present fails the witnessing requirement. Even if that were met: (1) a provision in a marriage contract purporting to limit a spouse's rights under Part II (Matrimonial Home) is unenforceable (s. 52 (2)), so Sofia's possessory rights in the matrimonial home cannot be given up this way; (2) a marriage contract may deal with the right to direct the education and moral training of children, but not the right to decision-making responsibility or parenting time (s. 52 (1) (c)), and in any event the court may disregard a domestic contract provision on parenting where that is in the child's best interests (s. 56 (1)); (3) the court may disregard a child support provision that is unreasonable having regard to the child support guidelines (s. 56 (1.1)). Finally, a court may set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it if a party failed to disclose significant assets existing when the contract was made, if a party did not understand its nature or consequences, or otherwise under the law of contract (s. 56 (4)); Liam's undisclosed account is relevant to the first ground.

story: Wei signed a separation agreement with his former wife in Richmond Hill two years ago. It was in writing, signed by both and witnessed. He waived spousal support in exchange for a larger share of the furniture. He did not get a lawyer. He has since lost his job because of a serious illness and now receives Ontario Disability Support Program income support. He wants the court to set aside the waiver and order spousal support.
question: Do I have a good chance of getting the court to throw out my support waiver?
modelAnswer: The site does not grade a claim or predict what a court will do; it can show you what the Family Law Act requires so you can prepare. The court may set aside a provision for support or a waiver of the right to support in a domestic contract, and order support, even if the contract says the support section does not apply, in three situations: (a) the waiver results in unconscionable circumstances; (b) the waiver is by or on behalf of a dependant who qualifies for an allowance for support out of public money; or (c) there is default in payment of support under the contract when the application is made (s. 33 (4)). Your facts touch (a) and (b): you would need to show the circumstances the waiver now produces, and evidence that you qualify for income support from public money (ODSP). Separately, a court may set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it for failure to disclose significant assets or debts, failure to understand the nature or consequences of the contract, or under the general law of contract (s. 56 (4)). If a waiver is set aside, the amount and duration of support are decided on the factors in s. 33 (9), including your needs, capacity to contribute to your own support, and health. Next step: gather the agreement, proof of your ODSP eligibility, medical information and a financial statement.

story: Last year the Ontario Court of Justice in Belleville ordered Trevor to pay Kayla $640 a month in child support. Trevor paid for three months, then stopped, and he now owes about $5,800. He works full time at a local warehouse. Kayla has been texting him reminders and is thinking of starting a Small Claims Court action to collect.
question: Who enforces a child support order like this one in Ontario, how is payment usually collected, and what can happen to Trevor's driver's licence?
modelAnswer: Under the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996, it is the duty of the Director of the Family Responsibility Office to enforce support orders that are filed in the Director's office and to pay the amounts collected to the person to whom they are owed (s. 5 (1)). Every support order made by an Ontario court must state that, unless withdrawn from the Director's office, it is enforced by the Director and amounts owing are paid to the Director (s. 9 (1)). An Ontario court that makes a support order must also make a support deduction order (s. 10 (1)), which is how payments are taken from a payor's income source such as an employer. When a filed support order is in default, the Director may serve a first notice telling the payor that his driver's licence may be suspended unless, within 30 days after the notice is served, he makes a satisfactory arrangement for complying and paying arrears, obtains an order to refrain and files it, or pays all arrears (s. 34). So rather than a separate lawsuit, Kayla's first step is to confirm the order and the support deduction order are filed with the Director's office.

story: Bernadette and Louis lived together in Sault Ste. Marie for eleven years without marrying. The house they lived in is in Louis's name; Bernadette paid for groceries, renovations and much of the household's day-to-day costs while Louis paid the mortgage. They have no children. Now that they have separated, Bernadette says: 'We were common-law for over ten years, so under the Family Law Act I get an equalization payment of half the difference in our property, just like a married spouse.'
question: Is Bernadette right that she can claim an equalization of net family property? What does the law provide for her instead?
modelAnswer: No. Equalization of net family property under Part I of the Family Law Act is between 'spouses', and the general definition of spouse means two persons who are married to each other, or who entered in good faith into a void or voidable marriage (s. 1 (1)). The wider definition that adds unmarried partners who cohabited continuously for not less than three years applies only 'in this Part', that is, Part III (Support Obligations) (s. 29). So Bernadette can claim spousal support as a spouse under Part III, decided on the s. 33 factors, but she has no statutory equalization claim. For property, the Supreme Court in Kerr v. Baranow explained that for unmarried persons in domestic relationships in most common law provinces, judge-made law was and remains the only option, and the main legal mechanisms are the resulting trust and the action in unjust enrichment. Her contributions to renovations and household costs are the kind of facts those claims look at.

three-year cohabitation definition applies to support only
